drills.label: Cold open
drills.question_line: SAM: Scenario five, Claude Code for Continuous Integration. A payments team runs an automated review
drills.answer_line: SAM: A. Include the prior findings and instruct the review
drills.stem: An automated review runs on every push to a pull request. After each new commit the same 11 comments reappear, and two flag problems the author already fixed. What should the team change?

options.A: Give the review the previous run's findings; report only issues that are new or still unaddressed
options.B: Have the posting script hash each comment's text and skip any comment posted before
options.C: Run the review only once, when the pull request is opened
options.D: Add "do not repeat earlier feedback" to the review prompt

drills.why: The model rewords findings, so hashes change, and a hash cannot know a problem was fixed. Only a review that sees its prior findings can judge that.

drills.label: Drill
drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. Code Generation scenario. A logistics team will replace its logging library
drills.answer_line: SAM: B. Sixty files and unknown wrappers are the plan-mode triggers
drills.stem: A team will replace its logging library across about 60 files. Some modules wrap the old logger in helper functions, and nobody is sure how many. What is the best approach?

options.A: Direct execution file by file, fixing each module as it comes up
options.B: Plan mode to map usage and design the migration, then carry it out with direct execution
options.C: A detailed prompt describing the new logging calls, run once in direct execution across the repo
options.D: Start with direct execution and switch to plan mode if the wrappers cause trouble

drills.why: 60 files and unknown wrappers are plan-mode triggers: plan the migration, then execute it. A means rework; C assumes a design; D waits for known complexity.

drills.label: Drill
drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. Choose two. Code Generation scenario. Claude Code has written a script that moves loyalty-programme accounts
drills.answer_line: SAM: B is right. D is the miss. The stem told you the conversion
drills.stem: Choose two. A migration script has three problems: no-tier accounts come out as "None" not empty; points are rounded before currency conversion, and the two steps interact; a log message has a typo. Which two approaches fix this most effectively?

options.A: Describe the rounding and conversion problem in one detailed message, because the fixes interact
options.B: A specific test case: an account with no tier in, an empty tier value as expected output
options.C: All three problems in one message ending "please be more careful with edge cases"
options.D: Ask for the rounding fix now, then the conversion fix later once rounding is correct
options.E: Ask Claude to rewrite the script from scratch from a longer description

drills.why: Interacting problems go in one message; one at a time is for independent ones. B names the failing case. C adds vague feedback; E throws away working code.

drills.label: Drill
drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. CI scenario. A review job runs Claude Code in print mode
drills.answer_line: SAM: C. The script needs machine-parseable findings
drills.stem: A review job runs Claude Code in print mode and a script turns its output into inline comments. About one run in ten, the script fails because the output is a paragraph of prose followed by a findings list. What should change?

options.A: Add a regular expression to the script that extracts the list from the prose
options.B: Add "respond with JSON only" to the prompt
options.C: Use the JSON output format with a schema for the findings
options.D: Retry the job when parsing fails

drills.why: Structured output enforced through the CLI with a schema. B is probabilistic; A works around the symptom; D repeats the unreliable call.

drills.label: Drill
drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. Choose two. CI scenario. A hospital software team's automated reviewer
drills.answer_line: SAM: B and C. B is categorical criteria with examples
drills.stem: Choose two. A reviewer posts about 40 comments per PR: naming preferences, possible-null warnings on values already checked upstream, and occasional real security issues. Developers now dismiss every comment. Which two changes best restore trust?

options.A: Add "only report findings you are highly confident in" to the review prompt
options.B: Explicit criteria: report bugs and security, skip naming and style, a code example per severity level
options.C: Temporarily switch off the possible-null category while its prompt is improved
options.D: Run the review three times and post only findings in at least two runs

drills.why: Categorical criteria with examples raise precision; switching off the noisy category restores trust now. A is the named confidence-word trap.

drills.question_line: SAM: Retrieval before the tease. Pause and name the three segments, and one technique from each.
drills.answer_line: ALEX: Plan mode against direct execution, with the Explore subagent.
drills.prompt: Name the three segments, and one technique from each.
drills.answer: Plan mode against direct execution, with the Explore subagent. Iterative refinement, five techniques. Claude Code in CI.
